idiom_name: guard clauses at the entry + immediate failure return + cleanup on every exit path
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: at every entry point where work is accepted, check the cheap conditions that decide whether the operation can be served (argument and state validity, admission capacity, dependency health) and hand the failure back to the caller immediately when one fails - do not queue, retry inline, or repair the state silently. Make the failure carry context (what was expected, what was found, which resource) and run the cleanup path before returning, so everything the attempt acquired is released. Reserve process-terminating aborts for invariants that are already broken beyond the request; recoverable refusals return to the caller, which owns retry/fallback policy. The classic structure is always hand-written here - there is no library that can decide what 'cannot be served' means for a given boundary.
pitfalls: Failing without a failure contract: each boundary invents its own signal, so callers cannot distinguish caller misuse from a transient fault and retry the wrong class of error.
Aborting after partial mutation with no cleanup path, so the refusal leaks exactly the resources it was supposed to free.
Logging the violation and continuing (fail-loud-only) leaves the system in the state the pattern exists to prevent.

Cascading fail-fast: two services both fail fast on each other's unavailability, causing a complete outage instead of graceful degradation — mitigated by circuit breakers and health-status awareness rather than binary presence/absence checks.

Fail-fast masking through flaky probes: a monitoring system that restarts containers on any failed probe amplifies transient infrastructure failures (CPU steal, noisy neighbor) into cascading restarts; probes must distinguish real unhealthiness from environmental jitter.

Test inconsistency: assertions that are enabled in tests (and therefore enforce fail-fast) are disabled in production builds, so the contract enforced during testing is different from production — always validate production builds include critical checks.

Premature fail-fast on hot paths: adding guard checks to latency-critical inner loops without profiling first can add measurable overhead; validate that the check is actually cheaper than the work it guards against.

Fail-loud-only without routing: failing fast by printing to stderr or a log file nobody monitors is a silent failure with extra steps — the "loud" half of fail-fast requires the signal reaches the right actor (on-call, developer, or downstream circuit) in time to act.

Fail-fast masking through catch-all handlers: an overarching try/catch that swallows all exceptions and resumes normal operation restores fail-slow behaviour while leaving the check in the code — audit handler scopes to ensure no handler bypasses the failure signal.

Fail-fast interacting badly with async cancellation: when a task is cancelled (Timeout, user cancellation), its cleanup path must not itself trigger a fail-fast abort — cancellation is a structured unwind, not a fault, and conflating the two causes double-abort cascades.

Premature fail-fast disguised as premature optimisation: adding guard checks to hot inner loops without profiling first can make the fast path slower — validate that the check is genuinely cheaper than the work it guards, especially in tight numerical loops.

Fail-fast with shared mutable state: refusing a request without cleaning up shared locks, permits, or partial writes leaves the system in a worse state than continuing — fail-fast and RAII/scope-guards must be applied together.

Gray-failure misdetection: a probe that marks a node unhealthy on any transient anomaly (CPU steal, noisy neighbour, GC pause) amplifies environmental jitter into cascading fail-fast restarts — probes must distinguish real unhealthiness from cloud-environment noise.

Confusing fail-fast with fail-over: failing fast on a dependency's unavailability does not trigger fail-over unless the calling system has a designed recovery path (fallback, alternative endpoint); absent that, fail-fast just propagates the outage.

Wrong move: applying fail-fast independently at every layer (HTTP handler, service, client) during a dependency failover -> each layer's instant refusal triggers the next layer's retry, so 3 layers multiply into 27 attempts and a 12-second leader election becomes an amplified outage -> instead classify infrastructure transients (leader election, DNS jitter) as retryable behind one bounded, time-boxed retry budget and reserve fail-fast for business-level violations.

Wrong move: short timeouts on every dependency call, treating every timeout as a crash -> gray failures (components that degrade slowly instead of dying) turn healthy-but-slow nodes into abort-and-restart storms, and the resulting retry feedback loop settles into a metastable state where throughput holds only while the system is impaired -> instead gate the abort on observed progress, not just elapsed time, and distinguish degraded from dead before refusing.

Wrong move: failing fast in a workflow that has already committed external side effects (payment charged, message published, record sent downstream) -> the abort cannot undo what the outside world already observed, leaving an inconsistency no finally/defer/RAII path can roll back -> instead place the abort point before the commit boundary, or make the failure path a designed compensating action rather than an exception.
